Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
How many illegal votes were cast in California’s last statewide election? I’m asking for a documented number, not an estimate of fraud you believe went undetected.
First, measuring fraud requires you to actually look for it and investigate it — neither of which is a priority of politicians right now in California. Second, whether you believe voter fraud is just a small problem or a big one, Prop. 39 is trying to solve a more serious and well-documented problem of public trust. A recent poll conducted by University of California, San Diego’s Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections showed 13% of Democratic voters have less confidence in elections than just two years ago — with 17% of Republicans and 16% of independent voters having less trust as well. Declining trust and confidence in elections is not a partisan problem — this is a democracy challenge that Prop. 39 fixes in a bipartisan way.

Of the documented cases, how many involved someone appearing at a polling place and impersonating another voter — the conduct that presenting ID in person would directly address?
First, your question incorrectly frames the problem Prop. 39 is trying to address — the dramatic decline in public trust in our elections. Polling consistently shows that a solid majority of Democratic, independent and Republican voters all say they would trust our elections more if we implemented Voter ID. Moreover, Prop. 39 will also ensure we improve identity verification for mail ballots by switching from the unreliable signature checks to the much easier four digits of a government ID.
Heritage describes its fraud database as a noncomprehensive “sampling” and makes no claim about the overall prevalence of fraud. Without comparing its selected cases with the billions of ballots cast, how can it establish that fraud is common enough to justify Prop. 39?
This question has now been answered twice above. You are missing the point of why Prop. 39 is needed — it is designed to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy. That is a big problem you seem to be ignoring here. With the polling showing declines in public trust — and support for reasonable voter ID requirements — why would you not want to implement Prop. 39 to improve trust and confidence in our elections?
California already establishes identity during registration and verifies mail-ballot signatures before counting them. What evidence shows these safeguards are failing often enough to require an additional check on every ballot?
First, Prop. 39 is about verifying identity when someone casts a ballot — not just when they register to vote. Second, a 2022 report by the Transparency Foundation showed an appalling lack of consistency in the signature checking process on mail-in ballots in many counties. Prop. 39 allows us to replace unreliable signature checks with an easier-to-use, four-digit PIN based on a government document of each voter’s choice.
The LAO estimates annual costs ranging from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. How many unlawful votes would Prop. 39 prevent each year, and what would taxpayers be paying per vote prevented?
The LAO cost estimate is wildly inaccurate and fails to account for the cost savings that would result by improving the accuracy of our voter rolls with saving on postage and printing of mail ballots. Prop. 39 will ultimately save money — while improving public trust and confidence in our democracy. Seems like a great return on investment.
The LAO says the measure could reduce registration among eligible voters who lack government-issued identification. How many eligible citizens is it acceptable to keep from voting to prevent one illegal vote?
This is absurd! Did requiring an ID to fly on an airplane reduce air traffic in the US? In states that have implemented voter ID, participation in voting has actually increased! Your question is grossly biased by falsely suggesting that citizens will be prevented from voting. Prop. 39 seeks to keep voting easy while improving identity checks in a balanced way to improve trust and confidence.
Prop. 39 requires “best efforts” to verify citizenship but does not define the term. Which government records are sufficiently complete and current to determine the citizenship of every registered voter?
First, it is not hard to define citizenship in the US — it is already well defined. Second, a variety of government databases exist to help election officials double check citizenship. That’s all Prop. 39 requires — which is why Prop. 39 is a balanced approach to implementing voter ID.
If government records cannot verify someone’s citizenship, does that person remain eligible to vote? If not, why should the government’s failure to find confirming information be treated as evidence that the person is ineligible?
Prop. 39 intentionally does not put any additional burdens on voters, which is why Prop. 39 specifically does not require that any voter provide documents to prove their citizenship to the government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.
A mail voter must provide the last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?

In recent years, heightened scrutiny has targeted the integrity of election processes, particularly regarding noncitizen participation in U.S. elections. We address here four frequently asked questions concerning noncitizen voting in American elections:
Can noncitizens vote?
Have there been documented cases of noncitizen voting?
How do election offices verify voters’ citizenship status?
What are the penalties for voting as a noncitizen?
Can noncitizens vote?
The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/ocomm/ilink/0-0-0-10948.html) explicitly prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. It is not legal in any state for a noncitizen to cast a ballot in an election for federal office. While federal law does not prohibit noncitizens from casting a ballot in state or local elections, no state currently allows noncitizens to vote in statewide elections. Municipalities in three states—California, Maryland, and Vermont—and Washington, DC allow noncitizens to vote in certain local elections. 1
San Francisco (https://sfstandard.com/2023/08/09/noncitizen-voting-school-board-san-francisco/) allows resident noncitizen parents and guardians to vote in school board elections.
Oakland passed a ballot measure in 2022 (https://ballotpedia.org/Oakland,_California,_Measure_S,_Noncitizen_Residents_Voting_Measure_(November_2022)) also giving noncitizen parents and legal guardians the ability to vote in school board elections. The measure is still pending implementation (https://oaklandside.org/2024/11/01/measure-s-noncitizen-voting-oakland-school-board-election/).
Several municipalities in Maryland and Vermont (https://ballotpedia.org/Laws_permitting_noncitizens_to_vote_in_the_United_States#Details_about_noncitizen_voting_in_local_elections) permit noncitizens to vote in municipal elections.
Washington, DC, began allowing noncitizen residents to vote in non-federal elections (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/laws/24-242) in 2022.
Election offices in communities that allow noncitizens to vote in local elections maintain processes to ensure that a registered noncitizen voter cannot vote for state or federal races. Maryland’s cities (https://www.npr.org/local/305/2022/11/09/1135568975/it-feels-very-welcoming-non-citizen-immigrants-on-voting-in-takoma-park), for example, maintain separate ballots for municipal elections. This ensures that noncitizens cannot receive a ballot for state or federal contests.
Have there been documented cases of noncitizens voting?
Illegal voting, including by noncitizens, is routinely investigated and prosecuted by the appropriate authorities, and there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.
When investigating noncitizen voting, it is important to distinguish between voter registration and casting a ballot. Noncitizen registration is already rare, and noncitizen voting is even less common.
Recent public debate has focused heavily on audits of voter registration lists, as these audits sometimes flag individuals who appear to be registered as noncitizens. ### What will the measure do?
Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected.
Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or “cure” a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it, as they are required to do when a voter’s ballot signature does not match what’s on file.
The measure also would require the state to provide free voter ID cards to eligible voters upon request, and state and county election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters using government data and publicly report the findings of that work.
Under current law, Californians are required to provide identification when registering to vote and must swear under penalty of perjury — a felony — that they are eligible to vote and a U.S. citizen.

Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Have there been documented cases of noncitizens voting?
Illegal voting, including by noncitizens, is routinely investigated and prosecuted by the appropriate authorities, and there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.
When investigating noncitizen voting, it is important to distinguish between voter registration and casting a ballot. Noncitizen registration is already rare, and noncitizen voting is even less common.
Recent public debate has focused heavily on audits of voter registration lists, as these audits sometimes flag individuals who appear to be registered as noncitizens. In many cases, however, further review shows the individual is in fact a citizen, and they were only flagged due to clerical errors or outdated records. For example:
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose flagged 521 cases of potential noncitizen voting (https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2023/09/27/ohio-sec-of-state-larose-flagged-more-than-520-cases-of-noncitizen-voter-fraud-only-one-was-legit/) between 2019 and September 2023. But an Ohio Capital Journal review (https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2023/09/27/ohio-sec-of-state-larose-flagged-more-than-520-cases-of-noncitizen-voter-fraud-only-one-was-legit/) found just one case in which a noncitizen was ultimately charged with voter fraud. The review noted that this was due to a combination of accidental registration and a lag in how the department of motor vehicles updates an individual’s citizenship status after naturalization.
Utah performed a citizenship review of its entire voter registration list (https://ltgovernor.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/CITIZENSHIP-FULL-SUMMARY-2.pdf) from April 2025–May 2026. After a time-intensive, multi-step review of more than 2 million registered voters, they identified only 27 confirmed instances of noncitizen registration. 2
Georgia : In October 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger announced that a citizenship audit of 8.2 million registered voters (https://georgiarecorder.com/briefs/georgia-gop-secretary-of-state-reports-audit-found-20-noncitizens-registered-to-vote-out-of-8-2m/) identified 20 noncitizens who had registered to vote. Of those 20 individuals, just nine had cast ballots in prior elections, most before Georgia implemented enhanced citizenship verification through the Department of Driver Services in 2012. The cases were referred to local prosecutors for investigation.
Nationwide, records from a federal citizenship verification tool (https://www.aclu.org/cases/bower-v-social-security-administration) show that just 0.04% of voter verification cases are returned as noncitizens.
In the rare instances in which noncitizens have been registered to vote—or have voted—the fault usually lies in administrative error. For example:
Oregon : Oregon officials in 2024 revealed (https://sos.oregon.gov/elections/Pages/DMV-Automatic-Voter-Registration-Error.aspx) that a clerical error caused 1,940 individuals to be added to the voter rolls, an unknown number of whom may have been noncitizens. Due to a poorly designed computer program, Department of Motor Vehicle workers mistakenly affirmed that these individuals had provided proof of citizenship when, in fact, they had not. Although it is possible that some portion of these 1,940 individuals were noncitizens, many were later found to be citizens. Nevertheless, given that only 44 of the 1,940 later voted, the clerical error could not have affected the outcome of any elections in a state that, in 2024, cast more than 2.3 million ballots.
Texas : Recently disclosed internal communications (https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/07/16/jane-nelson-concerns-save-data-voter-citizenship-uscis/) between former Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services reveal that the state mistakenly registered noncitizens to vote, even though these individuals had acknowledged their noncitizen status on a voter registration application.
New Jersey : On July 21, 2026, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill announced (https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/07/21/governor-software-error-non-citizens-register-vote/) that a software glitch in the state’s Motor Vehicle System caused approximately 6,600 ineligible noncitizens to be registered to vote, even though those individuals reported that they were not citizens during the registration transaction. The governor acknowledged that roughly 400 of these individuals cast ballots. However, there is no evidence to date that these votes altered the outcome of any races in New Jersey—a state that, in 2024, recorded over 4 million cast ballots.
While federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens in federal elections, prosecution typically requires demonstrating that the individual knowingly violated federal law. Therefore, the cases outlined above—of ineligible noncitizens being registered to vote through no fault of their own, and often without even their knowledge—are best addressed through administrative improvements. Such improvements, which can be found in a prior BPC report (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/modernizing-voter-list-maintenance-an-evidence-based-framework-for-access-and-integrity/), include investing in modern motor vehicle department and state election office technology and infrastructure; strengthening coordination and data-sharing between motor vehicle departments and voter registration officials; and expanding back-end verification processes, which use existing government data to verify the citizenship statuses of registered voters.
How do election offices verify voters’ citizenship status?
The National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra) requires that individuals registering to vote anywhere in the United States attest under penalty of perjury that they are a U.S. citizen.
Depending on the state, election offices then employ a combination of other tools to further verify status:
Review of documents that an individual used to obtain a state-issued ID or driver’s license. In states using this model, the motor vehicle department shares the types of documents a voter used to obtain an ID with the state or local election office. Those documents, such as a birth certificate or passport, can often confirm a voter’s citizenship. When they don’t, the election office can do additional investigation. 3
Use of federal data to verify citizenship. 23 states (https://www.uscis.gov/save/about-save/save-agency-search-tool?type_of_agency%5B%5D=5&benefit_category%5B%5D=97&benefit_category%5B%5D=98&items_per_page=10) have an agreement with the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services SAVE System to verify voters’ citizenship status.
Use of local and state data to verify citizenship. Election officials in some states also consult jury list dismissals (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/legislative-approaches-to-ensuring-only-citizens-vote) when the reason for dismissal is a lack of citizenship status.
For more on citizenship verification best practices, read BPC’s report, Modernizing Voter List Maintenance: An Evidence-Based Framework for Access and Integrity (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/modernizing-voter-list-maintenance-an-evidence-based-framework-for-access-and-integrity/).
What are penalties for voting as a noncitizen? Does voting by a noncitizen affect their immigration status?
There are significant penalties for registering or voting as a noncitizen. Illegally voting in a federal election can result in a fine and up to one year in federal prison (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-104publ208/pdf/PLAW-104publ208.pdf), and noncitizens found guilty of this crime may also face deportation and revocation of their legal status (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(D)Unlawful,on%20such%20violation.) under immigration law. Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(ii)Falsely,law%20is%20inadmissible.) for the purpose of registering to vote may also result in deportation or denial of future immigration status, even if no voting occurs.
The enormity of these penalties means that deterrence is an important factor in ensuring compliance with laws that prohibit noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The risk of deportation, jail time, and fines often deter intentional efforts by noncitizens to register and vote.

What GAO Found
The studies GAO reviewed on voter ownership of certain forms of identification (ID) documents show that most registered voters in the states that were the focus of these studies possessed the selected forms of state-issued ID, and the direct costs of required ID vary by state. GAO identified 10 studies of driver's license and state ID ownership, which showed that estimated ownership rates among all registered voters ranged from 84 to 95 percent, and that rates varied by racial and ethnic groups. For example, one study estimated that 85 percent of White registered voters and 81 percent of African-American registered voters in one state had a valid ID for voting purposes. The costs and requirements to obtain certain forms of ID, including a driver's license, state ID, or free state ID, vary by state. GAO identified direct costs for these forms of ID in 17 states that require voters to present a photo or government-issued ID at the polls and do not allow voters to affirm their own identities, and found that driver's license direct costs, for example, range from $14.50 to $58.50.
Another 10 studies GAO reviewed showed mixed effects of various forms of state voter ID requirements on turnout. All 10 studies examined general elections before 2008, and 1 of the 10 studies also included the 2004 through 2012 general elections. Five of these 10 studies found that ID requirements had no statistically significant effect on turnout; in contrast 4 studies found decreases in turnout and 1 found an increase in turnout that were statistically significant.
GAO conducted a quasi-experimental analysis to compare voter turnout in Kansas and Tennessee to turnout in the four comparison states that did not have changes in their voter ID requirements from the 2008 to 2012 general elections. In selecting these states from among 14 potential states that modified their ID requirements and 35 potential comparison states, GAO applied criteria to ensure that the states did not have other factors present in their election environments that may have significantly affected turnout. GAO selected states that did not experience contemporaneous changes to other election laws that may have significantly affected voter turnout; had presidential general elections where the margin of victory did not substantially change from 2008 to 2012 and all other statewide elections, such as U.S. Senate races, were non-competitive in both the 2008 and 2012 general elections; and ballot questions were not present, noncompetitive, or similarly competitive in both the 2008 and 2012 general elections. GAO analyzed three sources of data on turnout among eligible and registered voters, including data from official voter records and a nationwide survey. GAO's evaluation of voter turnout suggests that turnout decreased in two selected states-Kansas and Tennessee-from the 2008 to the 2012 general elections (the two most recent general elections) to a greater extent than turnout decreased in the selected comparison states-Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, and Maine. GAO's analysis suggests that the turnout decreases in Kansas and Tennessee beyond decreases in the comparison states were attributable to changes in those two states' voter ID requirements. GAO found that turnout among eligible and registered voters declined more in Kansas and Tennessee than it declined in comparison states-by an estimated 1.9 to 2.2 percentage points more in Kansas and 2.2 to 3.2 percentage points more in Tennessee-and the results were consistent across the different data sources and voter populations used in the analysis.
To further assess the validity of the results of this analysis, GAO (1) compared Kansas and Tennessee with different combinations of comparison states and with individual comparison states, and (2) controlled for demographic characteristics that can affect turnout, such as age, education, race, and sex. GAO also conducted an analysis using survey data on registrants from Kansas and Tennessee and a nationwide comparison group of all states other than the selected comparison states. These additional analyses produced consistent results. GAO's estimates are limited to turnout in the 2012 general election in Kansas and Tennessee and do not apply to other states or time periods.
GAO also estimated changes in turnout among subpopulations of registrants in Kansas and Tennessee according to their age, length of voter registration, and race or ethnicity. In both Kansas and Tennessee, compared with the four comparison states, GAO found that turnout was reduced by larger amounts:
among registrants, as of 2008, between the ages of 18 and 23 than among registrants between the ages of 44 and 53;
among registrants who had been registered less than 1 year than among registrants who had been registered 20 years or more; and
among African-American registrants than among White, Asian-American, and Hispanic registrants. GAO did not find consistent reductions in turnout among Asian-American or Hispanic registrants compared to White registrants, thus suggesting that the laws did not have larger effects among these subgroups.
A small portion of total provisional ballots in Kansas and Tennessee were cast for ID reasons in 2012, and less than half were counted. In Kansas, 2.2 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons, and 37 percent of these provisional ballots were counted. In Tennessee, 9.5 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons and 26 percent were counted. Provisional ballots cast for ID reasons may not be counted for a variety of reasons in Kansas and Tennessee, including the voter not providing valid ID during or following an election. GAO's analysis showed that provisional ballot use increased between the 2008 and 2012 general elections by 0.35 percentage points in Kansas and by 0.17 percentage points in Tennessee, relative to all other comparison states combined; these findings are not generalizable.
Challenges exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud. For the purposes of this report, "incidence" is defined as the number of separate times a crime is committed during a specific time period. Estimating the incidence of crime involves using information on the number of crimes known to law enforcement authorities-such as crime data submitted to a central repository based on uniform offense definitions-to generate a reliable set of crime statistics. Based on GAO's review of studies by academics and others and information from federal and state agencies, GAO identified various challenges in information available for estimating the incidence of in-person voter fraud that make it difficult to determine a complete picture of such fraud. First, the studies GAO reviewed identified few instances of in-person voter fraud, but contained limitations in, for example, the completeness of information sources used. Second, no single source or database captures the universe of allegations or cases of in-person voter fraud across federal, state, and local levels, in part because responsibility for addressing election fraud is shared among federal, state, and local authorities. Third, federal and state agencies vary in the extent they collect information on election fraud in general and in-person voter fraud in particular, making it difficult to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
In comments on draft report excerpts the Kansas, Tennessee, and Arkansas Secretary of State Offices disagreed with GAO's criteria for selecting treatment and comparison states and Kansas and Tennessee questioned the reliability of one dataset used to assess turnout. GAO notes that any policy evaluation in a non-experimental setting cannot account for all unobserved factors that could potentially impact the results. However, GAO believes its methodology was robust and valid as, among other things, GAO's selection of treatment and comparison states controlled for factors that could significantly affect voter turnout, and GAO used three data sources it determined to be reliable to assess turnout effects.
Why GAO Did This Study
The authority to regulate U.S. elections is shared by federal, state, and local officials. Congress has addressed major functional areas in the voting process, such as voter registration. However, the responsibility for administration of state and federal elections resides at the state level. In 2002 Congress passed the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), which requires states to request ID from first time voters who register by mail, when they register to vote or cast a ballot for the first time, and to permit individuals to vote a provisional ballot if they do not have the requisite ID. Numerous states have enacted additional laws to address how an individual may register to vote or cast a ballot. As of June 2014, 33 states had enacted requirements for all eligible voters to show ID before casting a ballot at the polls on Election Day.
GAO was asked to review issues related to voter ID laws. This report reviews (1) what available literature indicates about voter ownership of and direct costs to obtain select IDs; (2) what available literature and (3) analyses of available data indicate about how, if at all, voter ID laws have affected turnout in select states; (4) to what extent provisional ballots were cast due to ID reasons in select states; and (5) what challenges may exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
GAO reviewed relevant literature to identify 10 studies that estimated selected ID ownership rates. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also reviewed state statutes and websites to identify acceptable forms of voter ID in selected states and the price for certain forms of ID.
GAO also reviewed relevant literature and identified 10 other studies that estimated the effect of voter ID laws on turnout. GAO reviewed the studies' design, implementation, and analyses, and determined that the studies weresufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. Further, GAO compared turnout in two states-Kansas and Tennessee-that changed ID requirements from the 2008 to 2012 general elections with turnout in fourselected states-Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, and Maine-that did not. GAO used a quasi-experimental approach, a type of policy evaluation that compares how an outcome changes over time in a treatment groupthat adopted a new policy, to a comparison group that did not make the same change. GAO selected states for evaluation that did not have other factors in their election environments that also may have affected turnout, such as significant changes to other election laws. GAO analyzed three sources of turnout data for the 2008 and 2012 general elections: (1) data on eligible voters, using official voter records compiled by the United States Elections Project at George Mason University, (2) data on registered voters, using state voter databases that were cleaned by a vendor through data-matching procedures to remove voters who had died or moved, and (3) data on registered voters, as reported to the Current Population Survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau.
GAO also analyzed data from Kansas and Tennessee election officials on the number of provisional ballots cast for ID reasons in the 2012 general election, and data from the Election Assistance Commission's Election Administration and Voting Survey on the number of provisional ballots cast in select states in 2008 and 2012.
GAO reviewed relevant literature and identified 5 studies that attempted to identify instances of in-person voter fraud. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses, and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also interviewed election officials in 46 states and the District of Columbia and officials from federal agencies that maintain federal crime data to determine how, if at all, instances of in-person voter fraud are tracked in state and federal databases.

e government, as that is prohibited under current federal law. Instead Prop. 39 holds government officials accountable to double check citizenship using government databases.
A mail voter must provide the last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Summary
Support
Supporters argue that ID requirements at voting sites will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, and that most states require voters to show some form of identification to vote.
Oppose
Opponents say requiring ID will make it harder for eligible voters who don’t have a driver’s license or other supporting documents to vote. They say this will disproportionately affect those with disabilities, who are low-income or have recently moved.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Have there been documented cases of noncitizens voting?
Illegal voting, including by noncitizens, is routinely investigated and prosecuted by the appropriate authorities, and there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.
When investigating noncitizen voting, it is important to distinguish between voter registration and casting a ballot. Noncitizen registration is already rare, and noncitizen voting is even less common.
Recent public debate has focused heavily on audits of voter registration lists, as these audits sometimes flag individuals who appear to be registered as noncitizens. In many cases, however, further review shows the individual is in fact a citizen, and they were only flagged due to clerical errors or outdated records. For example:
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose flagged 521 cases of potential noncitizen voting (https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2023/09/27/ohio-sec-of-state-larose-flagged-more-than-520-cases-of-noncitizen-voter-fraud-only-one-was-legit/) between 2019 and September 2023. But an Ohio Capital Journal review (https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2023/09/27/ohio-sec-of-state-larose-flagged-more-than-520-cases-of-noncitizen-voter-fraud-only-one-was-legit/) found just one case in which a noncitizen was ultimately charged with voter fraud. The review noted that this was due to a combination of accidental registration and a lag in how the department of motor vehicles updates an individual’s citizenship status after naturalization.
Utah performed a citizenship review of its entire voter registration list (https://ltgovernor.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/CITIZENSHIP-FULL-SUMMARY-2.pdf) from April 2025–May 2026. After a time-intensive, multi-step review of more than 2 million registered voters, they identified only 27 confirmed instances of noncitizen registration. 2
Georgia : In October 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger announced that a citizenship audit of 8.2 million registered voters (https://georgiarecorder.com/briefs/georgia-gop-secretary-of-state-reports-audit-found-20-noncitizens-registered-to-vote-out-of-8-2m/) identified 20 noncitizens who had registered to vote. Of those 20 individuals, just nine had cast ballots in prior elections, most before Georgia implemented enhanced citizenship verification through the Department of Driver Services in 2012. The cases were referred to local prosecutors for investigation.
Nationwide, records from a federal citizenship verification tool (https://www.aclu.org/cases/bower-v-social-security-administration) show that just 0.04% of voter verification cases are returned as noncitizens.
In the rare instances in which noncitizens have been registered to vote—or have voted—the fault usually lies in administrative error. For example:
Oregon : Oregon officials in 2024 revealed (https://sos.oregon.gov/elections/Pages/DMV-Automatic-Voter-Registration-Error.aspx) that a clerical error caused 1,940 individuals to be added to the voter rolls, an unknown number of whom may have been noncitizens. Due to a poorly designed computer program, Department of Motor Vehicle workers mistakenly affirmed that these individuals had provided proof of citizenship when, in fact, they had not. Although it is possible that some portion of these 1,940 individuals were noncitizens, many were later found to be citizens. Nevertheless, given that only 44 of the 1,940 later voted, the clerical error could not have affected the outcome of any elections in a state that, in 2024, cast more than 2.3 million ballots.
Texas : Recently disclosed internal communications (https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/07/16/jane-nelson-concerns-save-data-voter-citizenship-uscis/) between former Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services reveal that the state mistakenly registered noncitizens to vote, even though these individuals had acknowledged their noncitizen status on a voter registration application.
New Jersey : On July 21, 2026, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill announced (https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/07/21/governor-software-error-non-citizens-register-vote/) that a software glitch in the state’s Motor Vehicle System caused approximately 6,600 ineligible noncitizens to be registered to vote, even though those individuals reported that they were not citizens during the registration transaction. The governor acknowledged that roughly 400 of these individuals cast ballots. However, there is no evidence to date that these votes altered the outcome of any races in New Jersey—a state that, in 2024, recorded over 4 million cast ballots.
While federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens in federal elections, prosecution typically requires demonstrating that the individual knowingly violated federal law. Therefore, the cases outlined above—of ineligible noncitizens being registered to vote through no fault of their own, and often without even their knowledge—are best addressed through administrative improvements. Such improvements, which can be found in a prior BPC report (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/modernizing-voter-list-maintenance-an-evidence-based-framework-for-access-and-integrity/), include investing in modern motor vehicle department and state election office technology and infrastructure; strengthening coordination and data-sharing between motor vehicle departments and voter registration officials; and expanding back-end verification processes, which use existing government data to verify the citizenship statuses of registered voters.
How do election offices verify voters’ citizenship status?
The National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra) requires that individuals registering to vote anywhere in the United States attest under penalty of perjury that they are a U.S. citizen.
Depending on the state, election offices then employ a combination of other tools to further verify status:
Review of documents that an individual used to obtain a state-issued ID or driver’s license. In states using this model, the motor vehicle department shares the types of documents a voter used to obtain an ID with the state or local election office. Those documents, such as a birth certificate or passport, can often confirm a voter’s citizenship. When they don’t, the election office can do additional investigation. 3
Use of federal data to verify citizenship. 23 states (https://www.uscis.gov/save/about-save/save-agency-search-tool?type_of_agency%5B%5D=5&benefit_category%5B%5D=97&benefit_category%5B%5D=98&items_per_page=10) have an agreement with the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services SAVE System to verify voters’ citizenship status.
Use of local and state data to verify citizenship. Election officials in some states also consult jury list dismissals (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/legislative-approaches-to-ensuring-only-citizens-vote) when the reason for dismissal is a lack of citizenship status.
For more on citizenship verification best practices, read BPC’s report, Modernizing Voter List Maintenance: An Evidence-Based Framework for Access and Integrity (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/modernizing-voter-list-maintenance-an-evidence-based-framework-for-access-and-integrity/).
What are penalties for voting as a noncitizen? Does voting by a noncitizen affect their immigration status?
There are significant penalties for registering or voting as a noncitizen. Illegally voting in a federal election can result in a fine and up to one year in federal prison (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-104publ208/pdf/PLAW-104publ208.pdf), and noncitizens found guilty of this crime may also face deportation and revocation of their legal status (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(D)Unlawful,on%20such%20violation.) under immigration law. Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(ii)Falsely,law%20is%20inadmissible.) for the purpose of registering to vote may also result in deportation or denial of future immigration status, even if no voting occurs.
The enormity of these penalties means that deterrence is an important factor in ensuring compliance with laws that prohibit noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The risk of deportation, jail time, and fines often deter intentional efforts by noncitizens to register and vote.

What are penalties for voting as a noncitizen? Does voting by a noncitizen affect their immigration status?
There are significant penalties for registering or voting as a noncitizen. Illegally voting in a federal election can result in a fine and up to one year in federal prison (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-104publ208/pdf/PLAW-104publ208.pdf), and noncitizens found guilty of this crime may also face deportation and revocation of their legal status (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(D)Unlawful,on%20such%20violation.) under immigration law. Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182#:~:text=(ii)Falsely,law%20is%20inadmissible.) for the purpose of registering to vote may also result in deportation or denial of future immigration status, even if no voting occurs.
The enormity of these penalties means that deterrence is an important factor in ensuring compliance with laws that prohibit noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The risk of deportation, jail time, and fines often deter intentional efforts by noncitizens to register and vote.

Highlights
What GAO Found
The studies GAO reviewed on voter ownership of certain forms of identification (ID) documents show that most registered voters in the states that were the focus of these studies possessed the selected forms of state-issued ID, and the direct costs of required ID vary by state. GAO identified 10 studies of driver's license and state ID ownership, which showed that estimated ownership rates among all registered voters ranged from 84 to 95 percent, and that rates varied by racial and ethnic groups. For example, one study estimated that 85 percent of White registered voters and 81 percent of African-American registered voters in one state had a valid ID for voting purposes. The costs and requirements to obtain certain forms of ID, including a driver's license, state ID, or free state ID, vary by state. GAO identified direct costs for these forms of ID in 17 states that require voters to present a photo or government-issued ID at the polls and do not allow voters to affirm their own identities, and found that driver's license direct costs, for example, range from $14.50 to $58.50.
Another 10 studies GAO reviewed showed mixed effects of various forms of state voter ID requirements on turnout. All 10 studies examined general elections before 2008, and 1 of the 10 studies also included the 2004 through 2012 general elections. Five of these 10 studies found that ID requirements had no statistically significant effect on turnout; in contrast 4 studies found decreases in turnout and 1 found an increase in turnout that were statistically significant.
GAO conducted a quasi-experimental analysis to compare voter turnout in Kansas and Tennessee to turnout in the four comparison states that did not have changes in their voter ID requirements from the 2008 to 2012 general elections. In selecting these states from among 14 potential states that modified their ID requirements and 35 potential comparison states, GAO applied criteria to ensure that the states did not have other factors present in their election environments that may have significantly affected turnout. GAO selected states that did not experience contemporaneous changes to other election laws that may have significantly affected voter turnout; had presidential general elections where the margin of victory did not substantially change from 2008 to 2012 and all other statewide elections, such as U.S. Senate races, were non-competitive in both the 2008 and 2012 general elections; and ballot questions were not present, noncompetitive, or similarly competitive in both the 2008 and 2012 general elections. GAO analyzed three sources of data on turnout among eligible and registered voters, including data from official voter records and a nationwide survey. GAO's evaluation of voter turnout suggests that turnout decreased in two selected states-Kansas and Tennessee-from the 2008 to the 2012 general elections (the two most recent general elections) to a greater extent than turnout decreased in the selected comparison states-Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, and Maine. GAO's analysis suggests that the turnout decreases in Kansas and Tennessee beyond decreases in the comparison states were attributable to changes in those two states' voter ID requirements. GAO found that turnout among eligible and registered voters declined more in Kansas and Tennessee than it declined in comparison states-by an estimated 1.9 to 2.2 percentage points more in Kansas and 2.2 to 3.2 percentage points more in Tennessee-and the results were consistent across the different data sources and voter populations used in the analysis.
To further assess the validity of the results of this analysis, GAO (1) compared Kansas and Tennessee with different combinations of comparison states and with individual comparison states, and (2) controlled for demographic characteristics that can affect turnout, such as age, education, race, and sex. GAO also conducted an analysis using survey data on registrants from Kansas and Tennessee and a nationwide comparison group of all states other than the selected comparison states. These additional analyses produced consistent results. GAO's estimates are limited to turnout in the 2012 general election in Kansas and Tennessee and do not apply to other states or time periods.
GAO also estimated changes in turnout among subpopulations of registrants in Kansas and Tennessee according to their age, length of voter registration, and race or ethnicity. In both Kansas and Tennessee, compared with the four comparison states, GAO found that turnout was reduced by larger amounts:
among registrants, as of 2008, between the ages of 18 and 23 than among registrants between the ages of 44 and 53;
among registrants who had been registered less than 1 year than among registrants who had been registered 20 years or more; and
among African-American registrants than among White, Asian-American, and Hispanic registrants. GAO did not find consistent reductions in turnout among Asian-American or Hispanic registrants compared to White registrants, thus suggesting that the laws did not have larger effects among these subgroups.
A small portion of total provisional ballots in Kansas and Tennessee were cast for ID reasons in 2012, and less than half were counted. In Kansas, 2.2 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons, and 37 percent of these provisional ballots were counted. In Tennessee, 9.5 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons and 26 percent were counted. Provisional ballots cast for ID reasons may not be counted for a variety of reasons in Kansas and Tennessee, including the voter not providing valid ID during or following an election. GAO's analysis showed that provisional ballot use increased between the 2008 and 2012 general elections by 0.35 percentage points in Kansas and by 0.17 percentage points in Tennessee, relative to all other comparison states combined; these findings are not generalizable.
Challenges exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud. For the purposes of this report, "incidence" is defined as the number of separate times a crime is committed during a specific time period. Estimating the incidence of crime involves using information on the number of crimes known to law enforcement authorities-such as crime data submitted to a central repository based on uniform offense definitions-to generate a reliable set of crime statistics. Based on GAO's review of studies by academics and others and information from federal and state agencies, GAO identified various challenges in information available for estimating the incidence of in-person voter fraud that make it difficult to determine a complete picture of such fraud. First, the studies GAO reviewed identified few instances of in-person voter fraud, but contained limitations in, for example, the completeness of information sources used. Second, no single source or database captures the universe of allegations or cases of in-person voter fraud across federal, state, and local levels, in part because responsibility for addressing election fraud is shared among federal, state, and local authorities. Third, federal and state agencies vary in the extent they collect information on election fraud in general and in-person voter fraud in particular, making it difficult to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
In comments on draft report excerpts the Kansas, Tennessee, and Arkansas Secretary of State Offices disagreed with GAO's criteria for selecting treatment and comparison states and Kansas and Tennessee questioned the reliability of one dataset used to assess turnout. GAO notes that any policy evaluation in a non-experimental setting cannot account for all unobserved factors that could potentially impact the results. However, GAO believes its methodology was robust and valid as, among other things, GAO's selection of treatment and comparison states controlled for factors that could significantly affect voter turnout, and GAO used three data sources it determined to be reliable to assess turnout effects.
Why GAO Did This Study
The authority to regulate U.S. elections is shared by federal, state, and local officials. Congress has addressed major functional areas in the voting process, such as voter registration. However, the responsibility for administration of state and federal elections resides at the state level. In 2002 Congress passed the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), which requires states to request ID from first time voters who register by mail, when they register to vote or cast a ballot for the first time, and to permit individuals to vote a provisional ballot if they do not have the requisite ID. Numerous states have enacted additional laws to address how an individual may register to vote or cast a ballot. As of June 2014, 33 states had enacted requirements for all eligible voters to show ID before casting a ballot at the polls on Election Day.
GAO was asked to review issues related to voter ID laws. This report reviews (1) what available literature indicates about voter ownership of and direct costs to obtain select IDs; (2) what available literature and (3) analyses of available data indicate about how, if at all, voter ID laws have affected turnout in select states; (4) to what extent provisional ballots were cast due to ID reasons in select states; and (5) what challenges may exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
GAO reviewed relevant literature to identify 10 studies that estimated selected ID ownership rates. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also reviewed state statutes and websites to identify acceptable forms of voter ID in selected states and the price for certain forms of ID.
GAO also reviewed relevant literature and identified 10 other studies that estimated the effect of voter ID laws on turnout. GAO reviewed the studies' design, implementation, and analyses, and determined that the studies weresufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. Further, GAO compared turnout in two states-Kansas and Tennessee-that changed ID requirements from the 2008 to 2012 general elections with turnout in fourselected states-Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, and Maine-that did not. GAO used a quasi-experimental approach, a type of policy evaluation that compares how an outcome changes over time in a treatment groupthat adopted a new policy, to a comparison group that did not make the same change. GAO selected states for evaluation that did not have other factors in their election environments that also may have affected turnout, such as significant changes to other election laws. GAO analyzed three sources of turnout data for the 2008 and 2012 general elections: (1) data on eligible voters, using official voter records compiled by the United States Elections Project at George Mason University, (2) data on registered voters, using state voter databases that were cleaned by a vendor through data-matching procedures to remove voters who had died or moved, and (3) data on registered voters, as reported to the Current Population Survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau.
GAO also analyzed data from Kansas and Tennessee election officials on the number of provisional ballots cast for ID reasons in the 2012 general election, and data from the Election Assistance Commission's Election Administration and Voting Survey on the number of provisional ballots cast in select states in 2008 and 2012.
GAO reviewed relevant literature and identified 5 studies that attempted to identify instances of in-person voter fraud. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses, and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also interviewed election officials in 46 states and the District of Columbia and officials from federal agencies that maintain federal crime data to determine how, if at all, instances of in-person voter fraud are tracked in state and federal databases.

In both Kansas and Tennessee, compared with the four comparison states, GAO found that turnout was reduced by larger amounts:
among registrants, as of 2008, between the ages of 18 and 23 than among registrants between the ages of 44 and 53;
among registrants who had been registered less than 1 year than among registrants who had been registered 20 years or more; and
among African-American registrants than among White, Asian-American, and Hispanic registrants. GAO did not find consistent reductions in turnout among Asian-American or Hispanic registrants compared to White registrants, thus suggesting that the laws did not have larger effects among these subgroups.
A small portion of total provisional ballots in Kansas and Tennessee were cast for ID reasons in 2012, and less than half were counted. In Kansas, 2.2 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons, and 37 percent of these provisional ballots were counted. In Tennessee, 9.5 percent of all provisional ballots in 2012 were cast due to ID reasons and 26 percent were counted. Provisional ballots cast for ID reasons may not be counted for a variety of reasons in Kansas and Tennessee, including the voter not providing valid ID during or following an election. GAO's analysis showed that provisional ballot use increased between the 2008 and 2012 general elections by 0.35 percentage points in Kansas and by 0.17 percentage points in Tennessee, relative to all other comparison states combined; these findings are not generalizable.
Challenges exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud. For the purposes of this report, "incidence" is defined as the number of separate times a crime is committed during a specific time period. Estimating the incidence of crime involves using information on the number of crimes known to law enforcement authorities-such as crime data submitted to a central repository based on uniform offense definitions-to generate a reliable set of crime statistics. Based on GAO's review of studies by academics and others and information from federal and state agencies, GAO identified various challenges in information available for estimating the incidence of in-person voter fraud that make it difficult to determine a complete picture of such fraud. First, the studies GAO reviewed identified few instances of in-person voter fraud, but contained limitations in, for example, the completeness of information sources used. Second, no single source or database captures the universe of allegations or cases of in-person voter fraud across federal, state, and local levels, in part because responsibility for addressing election fraud is shared among federal, state, and local authorities. Third, federal and state agencies vary in the extent they collect information on election fraud in general and in-person voter fraud in particular, making it difficult to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
In comments on draft report excerpts the Kansas, Tennessee, and Arkansas Secretary of State Offices disagreed with GAO's criteria for selecting treatment and comparison states and Kansas and Tennessee questioned the reliability of one dataset used to assess turnout. GAO notes that any policy evaluation in a non-experimental setting cannot account for all unobserved factors that could potentially impact the results. However, GAO believes its methodology was robust and valid as, among other things, GAO's selection of treatment and comparison states controlled for factors that could significantly affect voter turnout, and GAO used three data sources it determined to be reliable to assess turnout effects.
Why GAO Did This Study
The authority to regulate U.S. elections is shared by federal, state, and local officials. Congress has addressed major functional areas in the voting process, such as voter registration. However, the responsibility for administration of state and federal elections resides at the state level. In 2002 Congress passed the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), which requires states to request ID from first time voters who register by mail, when they register to vote or cast a ballot for the first time, and to permit individuals to vote a provisional ballot if they do not have the requisite ID. Numerous states have enacted additional laws to address how an individual may register to vote or cast a ballot. As of June 2014, 33 states had enacted requirements for all eligible voters to show ID before casting a ballot at the polls on Election Day.
GAO was asked to review issues related to voter ID laws. This report reviews (1) what available literature indicates about voter ownership of and direct costs to obtain select IDs; (2) what available literature and (3) analyses of available data indicate about how, if at all, voter ID laws have affected turnout in select states; (4) to what extent provisional ballots were cast due to ID reasons in select states; and (5) what challenges may exist in using available information to estimate the incidence of in-person voter fraud.
GAO reviewed relevant literature to identify 10 studies that estimated selected ID ownership rates. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also reviewed state statutes and websites to identify acceptable forms of voter ID in selected states and the price for certain forms of ID.
GAO also reviewed relevant literature and identified 10 other studies that estimated the effect of voter ID laws on turnout. GAO reviewed the studies' design, implementation, and analyses, and determined that the studies weresufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. Further, GAO compared turnout in two states-Kansas and Tennessee-that changed ID requirements from the 2008 to 2012 general elections with turnout in fourselected states-Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, and Maine-that did not. GAO used a quasi-experimental approach, a type of policy evaluation that compares how an outcome changes over time in a treatment groupthat adopted a new policy, to a comparison group that did not make the same change. GAO selected states for evaluation that did not have other factors in their election environments that also may have affected turnout, such as significant changes to other election laws. GAO analyzed three sources of turnout data for the 2008 and 2012 general elections: (1) data on eligible voters, using official voter records compiled by the United States Elections Project at George Mason University, (2) data on registered voters, using state voter databases that were cleaned by a vendor through data-matching procedures to remove voters who had died or moved, and (3) data on registered voters, as reported to the Current Population Survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau.
GAO also analyzed data from Kansas and Tennessee election officials on the number of provisional ballots cast for ID reasons in the 2012 general election, and data from the Election Assistance Commission's Election Administration and Voting Survey on the number of provisional ballots cast in select states in 2008 and 2012.
GAO reviewed relevant literature and identified 5 studies that attempted to identify instances of in-person voter fraud. GAO reviewed the studies' analyses, and determined that these studies were sufficiently sound to support their results and conclusions. GAO also interviewed election officials in 46 states and the District of Columbia and officials from federal agencies that maintain federal crime data to determine how, if at all, instances of in-person voter fraud are tracked in state and federal databases.

A mail voter must provide the last four digits of the government ID selected in the voter’s registration. What happens if an eligible voter transposes two digits, omits them, renews the ID or provides digits from a different valid ID?
Prop. 39 fixes a serious problem with the current mail-ballot verification process, which relies solely on signature matches — and some voters’ signatures have changed over the years and their ballots are being invalidated as a result. In the last election more than 100,000 mail ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches. Prop. 39 replaces that process with four digits from a government ID to ensure every eligible vote is counted — and allows a “curring” process if a voter transposes numbers to make sure every valid vote counts.
The proposition leaves the Legislature to decide which identifications qualify and what constitutes “best efforts” citizenship verification. Why should Californians amend their Constitution before knowing the rules that will determine whether their ballots are counted?
No, that is not true. Prop. 39’s reference to “best efforts” simply establishes the expectation that our county election offices do their best job in maintaining their voter rolls. The Legislature can help clarify that, but ultimately, Prop. 39 gives courts the authority to ensure proper compliance with the expectations voters are imposing to improve election management. California is currently not using widely accepted list management practices that are used in red and blue states across the country.
What elections in California over the last 100 years should be called into question because the number of illegal votes was officially found to be high enough to have swung the results?
This question is not relevant to the stated goal of Prop. 39 — which is to improve public trust and confidence in our democracy going forward. We are not engaging in conspiracy theories or accusations about stolen elections because that is exactly counter to our goal of restoring trust through widely supported bipartisan election integrity reforms.
What do opponents of Prop. 39 get most wrong?
Opponents of Prop. 39 falsely claim this is a Donald Trump scheme. Prop. 39 is absolutely not the same as Trump’s SAVE Act. Prop. 39 is the bipartisan alternative to implementing voter ID in a balanced way without burdens on voters — and with the singular goal of improving trust and confidence in our elections. We believe Prop. 39 will become the national model for how to get voter ID done in a bipartisan way, and California citizens need to lead the way where partisan politicians have failed us.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.
